posts.title: The first autumn hojicha, and why we roast it twice
posts.excerpt: The clay pan is back on the burner at the back of the shop. Here is why the October hojicha gets two roasts and a week of rest in between.
posts.content:
Every year there is one morning in October when the shop starts to smell of roasted chestnuts. That is the clay pan going back on the burner, with the first of the Kawai family's late-summer bancha in it.

Two roasts, one week apart

The first roast is quick and hot: it turns the green leaf brown and drives off the grassy edge. Then the tea rests for a week in paper sacks, and the flavour settles. The second roast is slow and lower, and it is the one that makes the cup sweet, like brown sugar and toast.

If you can smell it from the street, it's ready.

Hana, every October

Roasting also lowers the caffeine, which is why hojicha is the tea we pour after dinner and for anyone who comes in with a small child.

How to brew it

  1. Use 5 g of leaf (it is light and bulky, so a big spoonful) in a 200 ml pot.
  2. Pour water straight off the boil.
  3. Wait 30 seconds and pour it all out. A second cup needs another 30 seconds.

The first bags are on the shelf and in the shop now, and they will go into October's tea boxes too.

posts.title: Brewing sencha at 70°C: the one rule worth keeping
posts.excerpt: If green tea has ever tasted bitter to you, it was probably brewed too hot. A thermometer helps, but two cups do the same job.
posts.content:
Most people who tell us they don't like green tea have only ever had it made with boiling water. Sencha has a lot of sweetness in it, but it also has bitter catechins, and those come out much faster in hot water. At 70°C you get the sweetness and leave most of the bitterness in the leaf.

No thermometer? Use cups

Every time you pour hot water into a cold cup, it loses about ten degrees. So boil the kettle, pour into your teacups, pour from the cups into the pot, and you are close enough.

Bonus: the cups are warm when the tea goes in.

Then make it shorter, not weaker

If the cup is still too strong, brew it for less time rather than using less leaf. Less leaf makes thin tea; less time makes gentle tea.

posts.title: Yuzu season is coming: three sweets we make only in winter
posts.excerpt: From November the three old trees behind the shop are heavy with yuzu, and Teru's kitchen smells of nothing else. Here is what he makes with them.
posts.content:
The three yuzu trees behind the shop were here long before we were. They are knobbly, thorny and very generous: in a good year they give us more fruit than we can carry in one trip.

Yuzu monaka

Two crisp rice wafers shaped like flowers, filled with white bean paste folded with candied yuzu peel. Teru makes them on Thursdays.

Yuzu yokan

A firm jelly of white beans, agar and yuzu juice, cut in thin slices. It keeps well, which makes it a favourite for the tea box.

Yuzu nerikiri

A soft, hand-shaped sweet that looks like a tiny yuzu, down to the leaf. It only lasts a few days, so it is a counter sweet, mostly.

All three are best with a cup of Asahi sencha. We may be biased.

posts.title: A morning on the hill with the Hatano family
posts.excerpt: We walked the rows before the second picking with the family who grow our Asahi sencha, and stayed for lunch.
posts.content:
The Hatano farm is twenty-five minutes up the river road and then straight up. The rows of tea bushes follow the hill like a thumbprint, clipped into soft round hedges so the pickers can reach the tops.

We go up every spring to taste before we buy, and again in summer to see the second picking. This year the mist sat in the valley until almost ten, which the family says is why the leaf was so sweet.

The tea tastes like the morning it was picked.

Mr Hatano, pouring

Lunch was rice balls with pickled plum, and of course more tea. We came home with the bags for the autumn tea box and sunburnt necks.

posts.title: Whisking matcha at home (and why the whisk matters)
posts.excerpt: You can shake matcha in a jar and it will be fine. But a bamboo whisk is what turns it into foam, and it takes about fifteen seconds to learn.
posts.content:
Matcha is the leaf itself, ground to a powder, so you are not brewing it so much as suspending it in water. That is why it needs whisking: you are breaking up tiny clumps and folding in air.

The fifteen-second method

  1. Soak the whisk in warm water for a minute so the prongs bend.
  2. Sift 2 g of matcha into a warm, dry bowl.
  3. Add 70 ml of water at 80°C.
  4. Whisk fast from the wrist, in an M shape, for fifteen seconds.

The foam should be fine and even, like the top of a cappuccino. If there are big bubbles, keep going with the tip of the whisk just at the surface.

No whisk yet? A small jar, a lid and a good shake works too.

posts.title: Teaware for a small table: one pot, two cups
posts.excerpt: You don't need a cupboard of teaware. Here is the whole set we would start with, and why the side handle wins.
posts.content:
People often ask us what to buy first. Our answer is always the same, and it fits on a tray.

  • A side-handled kyusu, about 300 ml, with a fine built-in filter
  • Two yunomi, tall enough to hold in both hands
  • A tea caddy that closes well. Any tin will do.

The side handle looks odd at first, but it lets you pour with a small turn of the wrist, and you can share out every last drop between cups, which is the point.

Our Kihada teapots come from a small kiln in the next valley, glazed in the same yellow as our door.

posts.title: Cold-brew genmaicha for the last warm afternoons
posts.excerpt: Put the kettle away. Ten grams of genmaicha, a bottle of water and three hours in the fridge make the easiest tea of the year.
posts.content:
Cold water pulls out the sweet, savoury side of tea and leaves almost all the bitterness behind. Genmaicha is especially good this way: the toasted rice turns the cup nutty and round, like barley tea with a green edge.

  1. Put 10 g of genmaicha in a 500 ml bottle.
  2. Fill with cold water and close.
  3. Leave it in the fridge for three hours, or overnight.
  4. Strain and drink within a day. Top the leaf up once with more water.

A slice of yuzu in the glass doesn't hurt either.

products.name: Asahi Sencha
products.short: Our everyday sencha: bright, grassy and sweet, from the first spring picking on the Hatano family's hill. 100 g bag.
products.description:
Asahi means morning sun, and this is the tea we drink first thing at the counter. The Hatano family pick it in the last days of April, steam it lightly and roll it into fine dark needles that unfurl into a pale gold cup: fresh-cut grass, a little sweet pea, a clean finish.

Brew 4 g in 150 ml of water at 70°C for one minute, then again three more times, a little hotter and quicker each time.

products.name: Hillside Fukamushi Sencha
products.short: Deep-steamed sencha from the steep upper terraces: thick, emerald and soft, with almost no bitterness. 100 g tin.
products.description:
Fukamushi means deep-steamed. Steaming the leaf two or three times longer breaks it into smaller pieces that give up their colour and sweetness quickly, so the cup is a cloudy emerald green, thick and soft, with very little astringency.

It comes from the highest terraces of the Sugimura farm, where morning mist sits until ten. Brew it short: 45 seconds is plenty.

products.name: Twice-Roasted Hojicha
products.short: Autumn bancha roasted twice in our own pan: toasty, caramel-sweet and gentle enough for after dinner. 80 g bag.
products.description:
Every October we roast the late-summer bancha from the Kawai farm in a clay pan at the back of the shop, rest it for a week, and roast it again. The second roast rounds off the edges: the cup is amber, toasty and sweet, like roasted chestnuts and brown sugar.

Roasting also leaves it low in caffeine, so it is our evening tea. Brew with water just off the boil, 30 seconds.

products.name: Hikari Ceremonial Matcha
products.short: Stone-ground matcha from shaded spring leaves: vivid green, creamy and sweet enough to drink without milk. 30 g tin.
products.description:
Hikari is ground from tencha that grew for three weeks under straw shades, which keeps the leaves tender and sweet. Stone-milled slowly, it whisks up into a fine, creamy foam with a long, sweet, savoury finish.

Sift 2 g into a bowl, add 70 ml of water at 80°C and whisk in a quick M shape for fifteen seconds. Store the tin in the fridge once opened.

products.name: Yuzu Sencha
products.short: Asahi sencha with sun-dried yuzu peel from the trees behind the shop. Bright, citrusy, gone by spring. 80 g bag.
products.description:
In December we zest the yuzu from the three old trees behind the shop, dry the peel in the sun on bamboo trays, and fold it into our Asahi sencha. The cup smells of a winter morning: green tea first, then a lift of sour, floral citrus.

Made once a year, in small batches, until the peel runs out.

products.name: Genmaicha with Matcha
products.short: Sencha, toasted rice and a dusting of matcha: nutty, savoury and very easy to love. Also wonderful cold. 120 g bag.
products.description:
Half sencha, half toasted brown rice, with a little Hikari matcha shaken through so the cup turns a bright, cloudy green. It tastes of popcorn and fresh grass, and it forgives almost any brewing mistake.

In summer, put 10 g in a bottle of cold water and leave it in the fridge for three hours.

details.Brew cold: 10 g / 500 ml, 3 hours in the fridge

products.name: Kihada Kyusu Teapot
products.short: A side-handled teapot in our kihada yellow glaze, with a fine clay mesh filter. Holds 300 ml, two or three cups.
products.description:
Thrown for us by a small kiln in the next valley, glazed in the deep yellow of kihada bark. The side handle lets you pour with one easy turn of the wrist; the fine clay mesh inside holds back even deep-steamed sencha.

Each pot is made by hand, so the glaze pools a little differently on every one.

details.Care: Rinse with hot water, no soap

products.name: Pair of Yunomi Cups
products.short: Two tall everyday tea cups, one yuzu yellow and one matcha green, with a hand-combed wave around the middle.
products.description:
Yunomi are the tall cups you drink everyday tea from, holding them in both hands to keep warm. These two are glazed yuzu yellow and matcha green, with a wave combed around the middle while the clay was still soft, so your fingers find a grip.

Dishwasher safe, though they like a hand wash.

products.name: Matcha Bowl & Whisk Set
products.short: A wide pale-green matcha bowl, an 80-prong bamboo whisk and a bamboo scoop: everything you need to start.
products.description:
A wide, shallow bowl with room for the whisk to move, glazed the soft green of whisked foam; an 80-prong whisk carved from a single piece of bamboo; and a scoop that measures about one gram per heap.

Soak the whisk in warm water for a minute before you use it, so the prongs bend instead of snap.

products.name: Yuzu Monaka, Box of Six
products.short: Crisp rice-wafer shells filled with white bean paste and candied yuzu peel. Made by Teru on Thursdays.
products.description:
Monaka are two thin wafers of toasted rice with sweet bean paste between them. Ours are flower-shaped and filled with white bean paste folded with candied peel from the shop's yuzu trees: crisp, soft, sweet and a little sour.

Teru makes them on Thursdays and packs them in a paper box of six. Eat within ten days, with something green and hot.

details.Contains: Rice, white beans, sugar, yuzu peel

products.name: Seasonal Wagashi Box
products.short: Four soft nerikiri sweets shaped for the season, from pale blossom to yuzu, in a black lacquer-look box.
products.description:
Nerikiri are soft sweets of white bean paste and rice flour, coloured and shaped by hand. Each month Teru makes four for the season: this autumn a maple leaf, a chestnut, a ripe yuzu and a first frost.

Made to order and sent chilled on Tuesdays. Eat within three days.

products.name: Monthly Tea Box
products.short: Two seasonal teas, a wagashi and a letter from the counter, sent on the first Friday of each month.
products.description:
The box is how we share whatever we are most excited about this month: two teas of the season, 50 g each, one sweet from Teru, a brewing card and a folded letter from the counter.

This is a one-off box to try it; the monthly plans are on the tea box page. Sent on the first Friday of the month.

details.Inside: Two teas (50 g each), one sweet, a letter
